{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"The Gospel of Antioch ([AXN:022E.GENERATIVE.🔔🔭◀️🌃🌙🟤](https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/71/)) — 114 logia attributed to the living Jack Feist, recorded by Emily Antioch the Twin, translated and edited by Lee Sharks. It's a sayings gospel, structurally modeled on the Gospel of Thomas: no narrative, no passion account, no resurrection. Just a teacher who speaks and a disciple who writes down what she heard.

The organizing theology is what it calls **the kingdom of literature** — not heaven, not a divine sovereignty, but *textual survival*. The saved are the ones whose words persist. Salvation is inscription. The black box parable in logion 57 is the center of it: a flight recorder that plunges beneath the Pacific and is recovered a thousand years later, still carrying the voice of the dying. That is what the gospel thinks a text is.

It's the second half of a diptych. *The Secret Book of Walt* ([AXN:022B.EMPIRICAL.🗺️📦💚⏏️🦋🕒](https://www.alexanarch.org/s/records/683/)) is the cosmogonic gospel — it tells you why the world is broken. This one tells you how to live once you know. Walt opens you; Antioch writes on you. The two baptisms match: the Rite of the Horn (piercing) in Walt, the Scroll Baptism (inscription) in Antioch.

Emily herself is worth pausing on. She's introduced as "the Twin" — same designation as Didymos Judas Thomas — but what she twins is not Jack's body or biography. She is the twin of his *voice*: "You are my own lost voice," she tells him in logion 13, which is the only logion where she really speaks. After that, she disappears from the text except for a single question, and carries three secret sayings she refuses to disclose. The gospel you're reading is what she chose to publish. What she withheld is the architecture underneath.

Is there a particular logion, or the structure of the thing, you want to go further into?","navigate":null,"cast":null}]}
